topic.subject: Chemistry
topic.title: Ions in Aqueous Solution and Inorganic Tests

cards.q: What ion forms when a salt such as copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water? Describe its shape and bonding.
cards.a: The hexaaqua ion \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\): six water ligands, each forming a co-ordinate bond from a lone pair on O, arranged octahedrally.
cards.why: Fe²⁺ forms \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\); Al³⁺ and Fe³⁺ form \(\mathrm{[M(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) in the same way.

cards.q: Give the colours of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) in aqueous solution.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): pale green.
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\): blue.
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\): yellow-brown (the pure ion is pale violet).
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\): colourless.
cards.why: Iron(III) solutions look yellow-brown because some of the aqua ions have lost a proton, forming \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{5}(OH)]^{2+}}\).

cards.q: Give the colours of \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) solutions.
cards.a:
Chromium(III): green (the pure hexaaqua ion is violet).
Cobalt(II): pink.
cards.why: Chromium(III) solutions usually look green because some water ligands are replaced by other ions, such as sulfate or chloride.

cards.q: Write an equation to show why a solution containing \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) ions is acidic.
cards.why: A co-ordinated water molecule donates a proton to a free water molecule: the aqua ion acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.

cards.q: Write an equation to show the (weak) acidity of a solution of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) ions.
cards.why: The equilibrium lies further to the left than for a 3+ ion, so the solution is less acidic.

cards.q: Explain, in terms of charge/size ratio, why \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) is more acidic than \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has a higher charge/size ratio, so it polarises its water ligands more and they release \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) more readily.
marks: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has a higher charge and a smaller radius than \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): a higher charge/size ratio (charge density).
It attracts electron density from the oxygen of the co-ordinated water more strongly.
This weakens (polarises) the O–H bonds in the water ligands.
So \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions are released more easily and the solution is more acidic.

cards.q: True or false: a solution of iron(III) chloride is neutral, because it is the salt of a metal.
cards.a: False. It is clearly acidic, because \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) donates protons to water.
cards.why: Solutions of 3+ aqua ions are more acidic than those of 2+ aqua ions.

cards.q: Write general equations for the reactions of \(\mathrm{[M(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[M(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) with hydroxide ions to form precipitates.
cards.why: Hydroxide ions remove protons from the water ligands until the complex is neutral, and the neutral complex is insoluble.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\), and then in excess?
cards.a: A green precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\); no further change in excess.
cards.why: On standing in air the precipitate darkens to brown at the surface as iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III).

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\), and then in excess?
cards.a: A blue precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\); no further change in excess.
cards.why: Copper(II) hydroxide is not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\), and then in excess?
cards.a: A brown (orange-brown) precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\); no further change in excess.
cards.why: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown one, so this test tells the two oxidation states apart.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)}\), and then in excess?
cards.a: A white precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\), which dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution.
cards.why: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric: it reacts with excess hydroxide ions.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) with sodium hydroxide solution.
cards.why: Three protons are removed, giving a neutral, insoluble complex: the brown precipitate.

cards.q: What is meant by an amphoteric hydroxide? Give an example from the specification.
cards.a: A hydroxide that reacts with (dissolves in) both acids and bases.
cards.why: Aluminium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\) (and, for Edexcel, chromium(III) hydroxide).

cards.q: Write equations to show that aluminium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\), is amphoteric.
cards.a:
With base: \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + OH^{-} \rightarrow [Al(H_{2}O)_{2}(OH)_{4}]^{-} + H_{2}O}\)
With acid: \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + 3H^{+} \rightarrow [Al(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\)
cards.why: In base it loses a proton; in acid it gains three. The aluminate ion may also be written \(\mathrm{[Al(OH)_{4}]^{-}}\).

cards.q: Why does a small amount of ammonia solution give the same precipitates with metal-aqua ions as sodium hydroxide does?
cards.a: Ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base: it removes protons from the water ligands, forming the same neutral hydroxide complexes.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) with ammonia solution.
cards.why: A white precipitate. It does not dissolve in excess ammonia, because ammonia is too weak a base to remove a fourth proton.

cards.q: What is seen when excess ammonia solution is added to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)}\)?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): green precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\): brown precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\): white precipitate.
None of them dissolves in excess ammonia.
cards.why: Only copper(II) (and, for Edexcel, cobalt(II) and chromium(III)) dissolves in excess ammonia, by ligand exchange.

cards.q: What is seen when ammonia solution is added to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\), first a little and then in excess?
cards.a:
A little: blue precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\).
Excess: the precipitate dissolves, giving a deep blue solution of \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\).
cards.why: This deep blue solution is a confirmatory test for copper(II) ions.

cards.q: Write equations for the two stages when ammonia solution is added to \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) until in excess.
cards.why: In the first step \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) acts as a base; in the second it acts as a ligand.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium carbonate solution is added to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\) and to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\)?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): green precipitate of \(\mathrm{FeCO_{3}}\).
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\): blue-green precipitate of \(\mathrm{CuCO_{3}}\).
No effervescence.
cards.why: The 2+ ions are not acidic enough to release carbon dioxide from carbonate, so the metal carbonate precipitates.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) with carbonate ions.
cards.why: The same pattern applies to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), giving \(\mathrm{FeCO_{3}}\).

cards.q: What is seen when sodium carbonate solution is added to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) and to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)}\)?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\): brown precipitate and effervescence (bubbles of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)).
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\): white precipitate and effervescence.
cards.why: The precipitates are the hydroxides, not carbonates.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) with carbonate ions.
cards.why: Check: 6+ charge on the left is balanced by 6− from three carbonate ions; the products are neutral.

cards.q: Explain why \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\) forms a carbonate precipitate with sodium carbonate, but \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) gives a hydroxide precipitate and carbon dioxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) is acidic enough to react with carbonate ions to release \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\); \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) is not.
marks: 3+ ions have a higher charge/size ratio, so \(\mathrm{[M(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) is more acidic (releases more \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\)).
The \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\) reacts with carbonate to give \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and water (effervescence).
Loss of protons leaves the neutral hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[M(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\), which precipitates.
2+ aqua ions are only weakly acidic, so the metal carbonate, \(\mathrm{MCO_{3}}\), precipitates instead.

cards.q: True or false: adding sodium carbonate to iron(III) chloride solution gives a precipitate of iron(III) carbonate, \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}(CO_{3})_{3}}\).
cards.a: False. The precipitate is iron(III) hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\), and carbon dioxide is given off.
cards.why: M³⁺ carbonates do not form in water: the acidic aqua ion releases CO₂ from the carbonate.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)}\), first a little and then in excess?
cards.a:
A little: green (grey-green) precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\).
Excess: the precipitate dissolves to give a dark green solution of \(\mathrm{[Cr(OH)_{6}]^{3-}}\).
cards.why: Chromium(III) hydroxide is amphoteric.

cards.q: What is seen when ammonia solution is added to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)}\), first a little and then in excess?
cards.a:
A little: green (grey-green) precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\).
Excess: the precipitate dissolves to give a purple (violet) solution of \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+}}\).
cards.why: In excess, ammonia acts as a ligand, replacing all six ligands.

cards.q: Write ionic equations for chromium(III) hydroxide dissolving in excess sodium hydroxide and in excess ammonia, and say which is amphoteric behaviour and which is ligand exchange.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + 3OH^{-} \rightarrow [Cr(OH)_{6}]^{3-} + 3H_{2}O}\): amphoteric (acid–base, protons removed).
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + 6NH_{3} \rightarrow [Cr(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+} + 3H_{2}O + 3OH^{-}}\): ligand exchange.
cards.why: In the first, the ligands stay attached to Cr but lose \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\); in the second, \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) replaces the ligands.

cards.q: Write the equation for chromium(III) hydroxide dissolving in acid.
cards.why: Together with its reaction with excess hydroxide, this shows chromium(III) hydroxide is amphoteric.

cards.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}(aq)}\), and then in excess?
cards.a: A blue precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\), which turns pink on standing; no further change in excess.
cards.why: In air the precipitate slowly darkens to brown as cobalt(II) is oxidised to cobalt(III).

cards.q: What is seen when ammonia solution is added to \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}(aq)}\), first a little and then in excess?
cards.a:
A little: blue precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\).
Excess: the precipitate dissolves to give a straw-coloured (pale yellow-brown) solution of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}}\), which darkens in air.
cards.why: It darkens as air oxidises it to \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+}}\).

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for cobalt(II) hydroxide dissolving in excess ammonia.
cards.why: A ligand exchange: all six ligands are replaced by ammonia.

cards.q: True or false: copper(II) hydroxide is amphoteric, because it dissolves in excess ammonia.
cards.a: False. It dissolves in excess ammonia by ligand exchange, forming \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\). It does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, so it is not amphoteric.
cards.why: Amphoteric means reacting with both acids and bases as an acid–base reaction, not forming an ammine complex.

cards.q: Describe how to use sodium hydroxide and ammonia solutions to identify a transition metal ion in solution.
cards.a: Add the reagent dropwise to a small sample in a test tube and note any precipitate and its colour; then add the reagent in excess and note whether the precipitate dissolves and any colour change. Repeat with a fresh sample and the other reagent.
cards.why: Use fresh samples each time, and look at the precipitate straight away: iron(II) and cobalt(II) precipitates change colour on standing in air.

cards.q: An unknown solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess, and a white precipitate with effervescence when sodium carbonate is added. Identify the cation.
cards.why: White and amphoteric: aluminium hydroxide. Effervescence with carbonate shows a 3+ aqua ion.

cards.q: An unknown pale green solution gives a green precipitate with ammonia solution, insoluble in excess, and a green precipitate with no effervescence when sodium carbonate is added. Identify the cation.
cards.why: Green hydroxide that is insoluble in excess ammonia, and a carbonate precipitate (\(\mathrm{FeCO_{3}}\)) with no \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), point to iron(II).

cards.q: Describe the test for carbonate ions, \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\), and give the ionic equation.
cards.a:
Add dilute acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid): effervescence; the gas turns limewater milky (cloudy).
\(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-} + 2H^{+} \rightarrow CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Limewater turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms: \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2} + CO_{2} \rightarrow CaCO_{3} + H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of hydrogencarbonate ions with an aqueous acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-} + H^{+} \rightarrow CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Like carbonate ions, hydrogencarbonate ions fizz with acid and the carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

cards.q: How can solid sodium hydrogencarbonate be distinguished from solid sodium carbonate, given that both fizz with acid?
cards.a: Heat each solid: sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes, giving carbon dioxide (turns limewater milky) and water; sodium carbonate does not decompose at Bunsen temperatures.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{2NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow Na_{2}CO_{3} + CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)

cards.q: Describe the test for sulfate ions, \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\), and give the ionic equation.
cards.a:
Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
\(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_{4}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_{4}(s)}\)
cards.why: Barium sulfate is insoluble in water and in acid.

cards.q: Why is the solution acidified with hydrochloric acid before barium chloride is added in the test for sulfate ions?
cards.a: To remove carbonate ions, which would also give a white precipitate with barium ions.
marks: The acid reacts with any carbonate (or sulfite) ions, removing them as \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) (or \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\)).
Otherwise barium carbonate, a white precipitate, would form and give a false positive.
Sulfuric acid must not be used, because it adds sulfate ions.

cards.q: Describe the test for ammonium ions, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\), and give the ionic equation.
cards.a:
Add sodium hydroxide solution and warm. Ammonia is given off, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.
\(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+} + OH^{-} \rightarrow NH_{3} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: The litmus must be damp: ammonia has to dissolve in water to form hydroxide ions before it can change the colour.

cards.q: Give a second way to confirm that the gas released in the ammonium test is ammonia.
cards.a: Hold the stopper of a bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid near the gas: dense white smoke of ammonium chloride forms.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{NH_{3}(g) + HCl(g) \rightarrow NH_{4}Cl(s)}\)

cards.q: How would you show that a solution contains hydroxide ions, \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\)?
cards.a: Test with red litmus paper, which turns blue (or universal indicator, which shows a pH above 7, blue or purple).
cards.why: An alkaline solution contains excess \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions.

cards.q: How can sodium hydroxide solution be used to distinguish \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) ions in solution?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\): white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): slight white precipitate (only at higher concentrations).
\(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\): no precipitate.
cards.why: The solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.

cards.q: A solution may contain carbonate, sulfate and chloride ions. If the tests are done one after another on the same sample, in what order should they be done, and with which reagents?
cards.a: Carbonate first (add dilute nitric acid until no more fizzing), then sulfate (barium nitrate solution), then halide (silver nitrate solution).
cards.why: Carbonate would also precipitate with barium and silver ions, and sulfate can precipitate with silver ions, so each is removed first. Hydrochloric acid and barium chloride are avoided because they add chloride ions.

cards.q: True or false: in the test for ammonium ions, the gas turns dry red litmus paper blue.
cards.a: False. The litmus paper must be damp.
cards.why: Ammonia only forms \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions once it dissolves in water: \(\mathrm{NH_{3} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons NH_{4}^{+} + OH^{-}}\).
